Deadness
DED-nes
n. (the state of being past life or fruitfulness; of Sarah's womb, which Abraham considered and believed anyway)
From Old English dead. At Romans 4:19 it renders Greek nekrosis, a putting to death or state of death — a strong clinical word, used of Sarah's barrenness at ninety.

Biblical Definition

Paul is establishing that Abraham was justified by faith and not by works, and he refuses to make the patriarch's faith easy: And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sarah's womb. The Greek word is nekrosis — the state of a corpse. Paul applies it to the reproductive prospects of a hundred-year-old man and a ninety-year-old woman and does not soften it, because the whole argument depends on there being nothing whatever in the circumstances to encourage belief.

The verse says he considered not, which does not mean he failed to notice. Genesis records that Abraham fell on his face and laughed and said in his heart, Shall a child be born unto him that is an hundred years old? He had done the arithmetic. What Paul means is that having weighed the deadness, he did not let it be the deciding weight: He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God; And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform. Faith in Scripture is never the refusal to look at the facts. It is the conviction that the God who has spoken outranks them. And the same chapter identifies the God in question as the one who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were — which makes a dead womb precisely the sort of material He is known to work with.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): want of natural life or vital power; want of vigor; the state of being dead.

expand to see more

DEADNESS, n. Want of natural life or vital power; want of animation; want of warmth or ardor.

BARREN, a. Not producing young; not prolific; unfruitful.

QUICKEN, v.t. To make alive; to vivify; to revive or resuscitate, as from death.

PERSUADE, v.t. To influence by argument or expostulation; to convince by proof; to bring to a settled belief.

STAGGER, v.i. To reel; to waver; to begin to doubt; to hesitate; to become less confident.

Key Scripture

Romans 4:19 — "And being not weak in faith, he considered not his own body now dead, when he was about an hundred years old, neither yet the deadness of Sarah's womb:"

Romans 4:20 — "He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God;"

Romans 4:21 — "And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform."

Genesis 17:17 — "Then Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, Shall a child be born unto him that is an hundred years old? and shall Sarah, that is ninety years old, bear?"

Modern Corruption

Faith is redefined as a positive attitude that refuses to acknowledge difficulty, when Abraham's faith is described in the very verse that itemizes the impossibility.

expand to see more

A widespread teaching holds that to name a hard fact is to make room for unbelief — that a Christian should not speak of the diagnosis, the debt, or the barrenness, lest he undo the promise. Romans 4:19 destroys the idea in a sentence, because it is the Holy Ghost who lists the deadness. Paul names the age, the body, the womb, all three, and calls the man not weak in faith in the same breath. Faith that has not looked at anything is not faith; it is inattention. What Abraham did not do was let the facts overrule the word of the God who had spoken to him.

The verse also guards the character of saving faith itself. Paul's point in Romans 4 is not that Abraham had an impressive quality which earned him a son, but that he believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness — the righteousness reckoned, not achieved. This is the pivot of the Reformation doctrine of justification, and it hangs on the deadness: a man past fathering and a woman past bearing, so that when Isaac came there could be no question whose work he was. The same logic governs the sinner's salvation, and the same chapter names the God who does it — He quickeneth the dead.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek nekrosis (G3500), a state of death; nekroo (G3499), to put to death; zoopoieo (G2227), to quicken or make alive.

expand to see more

Greek nekrosis (G3500) — a putting to death, a dead state; used of Sarah's womb and of bearing about the dying of the Lord Jesus.

Greek nekroo (G3499) — to make dead; the perfect participle of Abraham's own body.

Greek zoopoieo (G2227) — to make alive; God quickeneth the dead in Romans 4:17.

Greek diakrino (G1252) — to waver, to be divided; he staggered not.

Greek plerophoreo (G4135) — to be fully carried, fully persuaded; Abraham's settled conviction.

Usage

"“neither yet the deadness of Sarah's womb” — the Holy Ghost itemizing the impossibility."

"“He staggered not at the promise of God” — the facts weighed, and outranked."

"“what he had promised, he was able also to perform” — the ground of the whole."
